slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: In “Ellen and Mary study botany,” the word and joins the two subjects Ellen and Mary.
In “Ellen or Mary studies,” the word or joins them in another way.
In “Ellen will study, if Mary helps,” the word if joins two whole clauses.
A word used only to join words or groups of words is called a Conjunction.

slides.text: A Conjunction is a word used to connect words, phrases, clauses, and members.
examples: over the hill and through the woods  (joins phrases)
I will go, if you come  (joins clauses)
and, or, but, if, because, since

slides.heading: Conjunction or Preposition?
bullets: Both are small joining words, but they work in different ways.
A Preposition shows a relation and always has an object:  “of wealth,” “by the house.”
A Conjunction merely connects; it shows no relation and needs no object:  and, or, but, if.
Test — can a noun follow it as its object? Yes → preposition; no → conjunction.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Conjunction
slides.instruction: Name the conjunction (or conjunctions) in each sentence.
items: He worked hard, but earned little.
I shall not go, if it rains.
Emma or Susan will stay home.
They submit, since they cannot win.
He is both kind and wise.
I stayed, because I was tired.
Study hard, or you will fail.

slides.heading: Practice — Conjunction or Preposition?
slides.instruction: Tell whether each joining word is a conjunction or a preposition.

slides.text: A Compound Element is two or more similar parts of the same proposition, joined by conjunctions.
examples: James and Samuel are kind.  (compound subject)
We run, jump, and play.  (compound predicate)
Dad owns a farm and a factory.  (compound object)
any part of a sentence can be compound

slides.heading: Kinds of Compound Elements
bullets: Compound subject:  “Ellen and Lucy are sisters.”
Compound predicate:  “We run, jump, and play.”
Compound object:  “Dad owns a farm and a factory.”
Compound modifier:  “Tray is a large, black, and friendly dog.”
The conjunction may be written out, or simply understood.

slides.heading: Practice — What Is Compound?
slides.instruction: Tell which part is compound: the subject, the predicate, or the object.
items: Dad owns a farm and a factory.

slides.heading: Commas in a Series
bullets: When three or more parts are joined, use commas to separate them.
Put a comma after each part, and the conjunction before the last:  “red, white, and blue.”
When only two parts are joined, use just the conjunction — no comma:  “salt and pepper.”
Ex. — “She is kind, honest, and brave.”  ·  “We run and jump.”

slides.heading: Practice — Punctuate the Series
slides.instruction: Write each list as a correct series, with commas and “and.”

items: How does a conjunction differ from a preposition?
Name some kinds of compound elements.
In a series of three, where does the conjunction go?
answers: A word used to connect words, phrases, clauses, or members.
And, or, but, if, because, since.
A conjunction merely connects; a preposition shows a relation and has an object.
Two or more similar parts of a proposition joined by conjunctions.
Before the last part — “red, white, and blue.”
